topic.reason: הנושא נקבע לפי התוכנית השבועית של 2026-10-25 (משבצת 3 מתוך 7, כל חבילה על נושא אחר). ילד שחוזר מהגן ואומר ״לא שיתפו אותי״ הוא רגע מוכר בכל תקופה בשנה ולכן אין כאן טענה על לוח שנה. בקטלוג יש ספר על חברות אמיתית לגילאי 4 עד 8 (אור והסוד שבים, ספר 20) ולכן סיפור אישי בסוף הוא המשך טבעי. רגיש: לא לרמוז על בריונות ולא להאשים ילדים אחרים או את ההורה; רק סימן אחד ברור מתי לפנות לגננת.

sources.title: 8 Ways to Help Your Child When They're Being Excluded
sources.publisher: Banner Health (Regan Olsson, with Adeola Adelayo, MD, psychiatrist at Banner Behavioral Health Hospital), 6 June 2021
sources.quote: try not to react too quickly ... Encourage them to talk and then let them talk ... don't interrupt, criticize or diminish what they're sharing with you. 2. Validate feelings When they're done sharing, validate their feelings and demonstrate you understand how they feel. ... Tell and show your child that they are unconditionally loved and valued by their family.
sources.supports: When a child is left out: listen without interrupting or diminishing, then validate the feeling; show the child they are loved at home. Written mostly about school-age children; applied to a 4 year old as a related situation.

sources.title: Social Development in Preschoolers: Learning How to Share & Cooperate
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 5 Dec 2024)
sources.quote: Help your child with the appropriate words to describe their feelings and desires so that they don't feel frustrated.
sources.supports: Giving preschoolers words for their feelings and wishes.

sources.title: Supporting your child to make friends (Tips for Parents)
sources.publisher: Welsh Government, 2024 (WG50353)
sources.quote: Others might get upset if they feel left out ... You can help them at home by role playing with toys ... Read books about friendships with your child ... This is a really simple but very effective way of helping children to understand friendships and what to do if the friends have conflict or fall out. ... Set aside some one-to-one time everyday to ask how their day went and how they are feeling. Bedtime can be a good time for this.
sources.supports: Children in nursery or school who feel left out: role play with toys at home, daily one-to-one time to talk (bedtime is a good time), and reading books about friendships.

sources.title: Helping Kids Cope With Cliques
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Elenda T. Hessel, PhD, June 2023)
sources.quote: And some may be in today and out tomorrow. ... Help put rejection in perspective. Remind your child of times they've been angry with parents, friends, or siblings ... how quickly things can change.
sources.supports: Who is in and who is out can change from day to day; help the child see that things change quickly. Written about cliques in older children; applied to a gan day as a related situation.

sources.title: 'We're friends, right?': Children's use of access rituals in a nursery school
sources.publisher: William A. Corsaro, Language in Society 8 (2-3), 1979, pp. 315-336, Cambridge University Press (abstract read)
sources.quote: The findings show that entry into play is a production of some importance involving considerable time and strategy to accomplish, while leave-taking usually involves unmarked physical movement from play areas. The importance of peer interaction in the acquisition of access rituals and the necessity of studying children's verbal routines in natural settings are discussed.
sources.supports: In a nursery school, getting into a game takes considerable time and strategy, and children acquire these entry routines through peer interaction. One observational study from 1979.

sources.title: 8 Ways to Help Your Child When They're Being Excluded
sources.publisher: Banner Health (Regan Olsson, with Adeola Adelayo, MD, psychiatrist at Banner Behavioral Health Hospital), 6 June 2021
sources.quote: Encourage them to talk and then let them talk ... When they're done sharing, validate their feelings and demonstrate you understand how they feel.
sources.supports: Ask and let the child talk, then validate the feeling. Mostly school-age context, applied as related.

sources.title: Supporting your child to make friends (Tips for Parents)
sources.publisher: Welsh Government, 2024 (WG50353)
sources.quote: You can help them at home by role playing with toys ... You can help them to develop a 'script' that encourages sharing and keeping friends e.g., "when you have finished playing with the toy can I play with it" ... Be a great role model ... When you are with other adults, practice talking and listening ... you could say "hello" to the other child and their parent so that your child learns a simple but effective skill to make the first step. ... Try to stand back and let kids work out their differences for themselves at first ... Try suggesting they approach the children with a new game that they can all play together. ... Read books about friendships with your child
sources.supports: Role play with toys, a ready script for joining and for a turn, parents as role models, saying hello first at the park, standing back at first, suggesting a new game everyone can play, and reading books about friendships.

It can be really helpful to arrange play dates at your house where your child feels most relaxed. ... Read books about friendships with your child
sources.supports: Daily one-to-one time (bedtime), suggesting a new game everyone can play, play dates at home, and reading books about friendships.

sources.title: 'We're friends, right?': Children's use of access rituals in a nursery school
sources.publisher: William A. Corsaro, Language in Society 8 (2-3), 1979, pp. 315-336, Cambridge University Press (abstract read)
sources.quote: The findings show that entry into play is a production of some importance involving considerable time and strategy to accomplish, while leave-taking usually involves unmarked physical movement from play areas. The importance of peer interaction in the acquisition of access rituals and the necessity of studying children's verbal routines in natural settings are discussed.
sources.supports: In a nursery school, getting into a game takes considerable time and strategy, and children acquire entry routines through peer interaction. One observational study from 1979; the slide says it as a possibility for this girl.

sources.title: Supporting your child to make friends (Tips for Parents)
sources.publisher: Welsh Government, 2024 (WG50353)
sources.quote: You can help them at home by role playing with toys ... You can help them to develop a 'script' that encourages sharing and keeping friends e.g., "when you have finished playing with the toy can I play with it" and "can we all play together as friends today so that nobody feels left out". ... When you are with other adults, practice talking and listening ... you could say "hello" to the other child and their parent so that your child learns a simple but effective skill to make the first step. ... Try to stand back and let kids work out their differences for themselves at first ... Try suggesting they approach the children with a new game that they can all play together. ... Read books about friendships with your child
sources.supports: Role play with toys, a ready script to join and to ask for a turn, a new game everyone can play, saying hello first, parents modelling conversation, standing back at first, and reading books about friendships.

sources.title: What to Do If Your Child Hasn't Made Friends at Preschool
sources.publisher: First 5 California
sources.quote: Try acting out different scenarios where they can practice taking turns, sharing toys, playing together, and listening.
sources.supports: Practising taking turns and playing together at home.

sources.title: Social Development in Preschoolers: Learning How to Share & Cooperate
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 5 Dec 2024)
sources.quote: Your child will learn to take turns and share toys in small groups. ... However, particularly in the beginning, you'll need to encourage this cooperation.
sources.supports: Preschoolers learn to take turns, and parents need to encourage it at first.

sources.title: 8 Ways to Help Your Child When They're Being Excluded
sources.publisher: Banner Health (Regan Olsson, with Adeola Adelayo, MD, psychiatrist at Banner Behavioral Health Hospital), 6 June 2021
sources.quote: it doesn't matter how well-adjusted or well-liked they are, they are bound to feel left out at some point in time. ... try not to react too quickly ... Remind them of the healthy relationships and friendships they do have with others
sources.supports: Even well-liked children feel left out at some point; do not react too quickly; remind them of the friendships they do have. Mostly school-age context, applied as related.

sources.title: Supporting your child to make friends (Tips for Parents)
sources.publisher: Welsh Government, 2024 (WG50353)
sources.quote: Falling out is completely normal. ... You can also try to encourage them to play with other children in their class to see what fun things they are doing. ... Arguments and falling out are very normal but if you notice your child is getting upset, becoming withdrawn and not wanting to go to school they may be feeling left out a lot or being bullied. If in doubt, speak to their teacher or key worker in nursery. They will be in the best position to watch your child interact every day ... Read books about friendships with your child
sources.supports: Falling out is normal; encourage playing with other children in the class; signs to watch (upset, withdrawn, not wanting to go) and talking to the nursery teacher; reading books about friendships.

sources.title: What to Do If Your Child Hasn't Made Friends at Preschool
sources.publisher: First 5 California
sources.quote: Trying new sports, arts and crafts, or music can help your child meet other children with similar interests.
sources.supports: Activities outside preschool help the child meet other children.

sources.title: Helping Kids Cope With Cliques
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Elenda T. Hessel, PhD, June 2023)
sources.quote: Keep social circles open and diverse. Encourage kids to be friends with people they like and enjoy from different settings, backgrounds, ages, and interests. ... These kinds of activities give them a chance to create another social group and learn new skills.
sources.supports: Friends from different settings and activities outside school give another social group. Older-child context, applied as related.
